summary: Describes using elliptic curve cryptography in the SSH transport protocol, specifying ECDH and ECMQV key agreement and ECDSA for signatures.

eli5.summary: SSH needs ways to agree on a secret and prove who you are. This adds shorter, quicker mathematical tricks for both.

subtitle: How SSH adopted elliptic curve key exchange and signatures: ECDH, ECMQV and ECDSA.

tldr.problem: SSH needed public-key algorithms that give strong security with small keys, and the elliptic curve family was becoming widely used.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines ecdsa-sha2-* host keys and signatures, ecdh-sha2-* key exchange and an optional ecmqv-sha2 key exchange, with named curves and SHA2 hashes chosen by curve size.
tldr.outcome: Every compliant implementation MUST support the ecdsa-sha2-* key format and ECDH key exchange on three required NIST curves. Servers that do not know the new names just skip them during negotiation.

today: RFC 5656 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Elliptic Curves in SSH
sections.content:
RFC 5656 adds Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key exchange, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) and, as an option, Elliptic Curve Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (ECMQV) key agreement to the SSH transport layer. It also uses the SHA2 family of hash functions.

The motivation is key size. Elliptic curve versions of RSA, DSA and Diffie-Hellman give equivalent security with smaller keys. The RFC's table, based on NIST 800-57, pairs a 128-bit symmetric strength with a 3072-bit RSA key and a 256 to 383 bit ECC key.

The document only covers the SSH integration. The underlying cryptography is left to other standards, mainly SEC 1. Implementers need to know SSH (RFC 4251, RFC 4253, RFC 4250) and ECC.
sections.eli5: A small key that is just as hard to pick as a big one is easier to carry around. Elliptic curves give SSH those small, strong keys.

sections.title: The ECC Public Key Algorithm
sections.content:
The ecdsa-sha2-* family defines both the host key format and the signature format. Every compliant SSH ECC implementation MUST implement it.

A key is encoded as the string ecdsa-sha2-[identifier] followed by a blob holding the curve identifier and Q, the public key point encoded as an octet string as in SEC 1. Point compression MAY be used.

Signatures are made with ECDSA. They are encoded as the same ecdsa-sha2-[identifier] string followed by a blob of two mpint values, r and s. The message hash MUST come from the SHA2 family, chosen by curve size.
sections.eli5: The key says which curve it uses, and a signature is two big numbers that only the key owner could have produced.

sections.title: ECDH and ECMQV Key Exchange
sections.content:
In ECDH key exchange both sides make an ephemeral key pair and combine their private key with the other side's public key to get a shared secret. The server signs the exchange hash, so it is explicitly authenticated. Every compliant implementation MUST implement ECDH.

The client sends SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT with its ephemeral public key Q_C. The server replies with SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY carrying its host key K_S, its ephemeral key Q_S and a signature on the exchange hash. The exchange hash covers both identification strings, both SSH_MSG_KEXINIT payloads, the host key, both ephemeral keys and the shared secret K.

All received elliptic curve public keys MUST be validated, and if validation fails the key exchange MUST fail. The client is RECOMMENDED to check that the host key really belongs to the server. Accepting it unchecked makes the protocol insecure against active attacks.

ECMQV is OPTIONAL. It uses the server's long-term host key together with ephemeral keys, which gives implicit server authentication, so it can only be chosen if an ECC host key algorithm is also chosen. Instead of a signature, the server sends an HMAC tag computed on the hash using the shared secret. The client uses one ephemeral key as both of its keys, which the RFC says is more efficient and does not hurt security.
sections.eli5: Both sides mix a secret number with the other side's public number and end up with the same secret, without ever sending it. The server then proves it is the real server.

sections.title: Method Names and Curve Identifiers
sections.content:
Three required NIST curves use plain identifiers: nistp256, nistp384 and nistp521. Implementations MUST use these strings for them even if an OID exists. For every other curve, the identifier is the period-separated decimal form of its ASN.1 object identifier, as long as the combined name stays within the 64-character limit of the SSH architecture.

Names are built by concatenation: ecdsa-sha2- plus the identifier for host keys, and ecdh-sha2- plus the identifier for key exchange. For example, ECDH on sect409k1 is ecdh-sha2-1.3.132.0.36. ECMQV has a single name, ecmqv-sha2, because the curve comes from the host key algorithm.

The SHA2 variant is picked from the curve size.
sections.eli5: Each method gets a name made by sticking the curve's name on the end, like labeling a jar with what is inside.

sections.title: Required and Recommended Curves
sections.content:
Every SSH ECC implementation MUST support the three required curves nistp256 (secp256r1), nistp384 (secp384r1) and nistp521 (secp521r1). They SHOULD stay enabled unless local security policy disables them.

Implementations are also RECOMMENDED to support nine more curves from SEC 2: nistk163, nistp192, nistp224, nistk233, nistb233, nistk283, nistk409, nistb409 and nistt571. Any other curve with an ASN.1 OID MAY be supported.

Implementers SHOULD let administrators disable curves, including required and recommended ones, to meet local policy.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to know three standard curves so they can always find one in common. A few more are suggested as extras.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The best known way to break all three mechanisms is to solve the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, and the best known general algorithm is the Pollard-rho method. The RFC notes that Shor's algorithm could solve the problem on a large quantum computer, but says such machines had not been built and it was widely believed to be at least 20 years away at the time of writing.

Roughly, an N-bit curve offers the security of an N/2-bit symmetric cipher, so the 256-bit nistp256 curve suits 128-bit AES. Implementations SHOULD NOT use curves smaller than 160 bits. Administrators should be cautious about enabling curves outside the listed ones, because not all curves are secure.

Curve size should match the other parts of the handshake, such as host key size, hash and bulk cipher. Implementers SHOULD generate ephemeral private keys and the ECDSA value k from a properly seeded random generator, protect them from leakage, never reuse them and erase them when no longer needed.
sections.eli5: A lock is only as strong as its weakest part, so the curve size, hash and cipher should all be about equally strong. Secret random numbers must be truly random and thrown away afterwards.

sections.title: Compatibility and Manageability
sections.content:
Because SSH negotiates algorithms, an implementation that does not recognise the new names ignores them and uses the next mutually supported method, so backward compatibility is not harmed.

The RFC also expects no significant computational burden on servers. Thanks to smaller keys, elliptic curve cryptography can be implemented more efficiently than RSA, finite field Diffie-Hellman or DSA at the same security level.

The IANA section registers the ecdsa-sha2- and ecdh-sha2- name families and the single name ecmqv-sha2, and creates no new registries. Key exchange message numbers 30 and 31 are reused by both ECDH and ECMQV.
sections.eli5: If a computer does not know the new trick, SSH just picks an older trick they both know, so nothing breaks.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT
messages.note: Carries the client's ephemeral public key Q_C.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY
messages.note: Host key K_S, ephemeral key Q_S and a signature on the exchange hash.
